title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:30–33)
hookLine: a new covenant: "in their heart will I write it"
carry: a line no exile can carry off

cards: Torah gets written on a lot of surfaces. On tablets of stone, carried down a mountain. On parchment, rolled into a scroll and lifted in the synagogue.
On a tiny scroll tucked into a case on a doorpost, because Deuteronomy says to write these words upon the posts of thy house. Ink, stone, wood.
Every one of them can be lost, broken, or left behind when you're carried into exile. In the middle of his chapters of comfort, Jeremiah names one more surface, one that goes wherever you go.

teach.b: Here's the promise. "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah."
Not like the covenant made with their ancestors on the day God took them by the hand out of Egypt, which they broke.

teach.h: IN THEIR HEARTS WILL I WRITE IT.
teach.b: And then: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." My law: in Hebrew, torati, my Torah, my teaching.
The text doesn't promise a new set of words.

teach.h: THE SAME TEACHING, A NEW PLACE.
teach.b: It's the same teaching, in a new place. Not outside you, on stone, where you have to go and read it, but inside, simply part of who you are.

Deuteronomy already reaches for this: these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart. Proverbs says it too: write them upon the table of thine heart. Jeremiah's twist is who does the writing.

teach.h: FROM THE LEAST TO THE GREATEST.
teach.b: And the next verse draws out what that would mean: no one will need to teach a neighbor, "for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest."
Some Jewish readers hear this as the hope of a day when Torah is so deeply learned that it's second nature, like a language you grew up speaking.
There's a small version within reach of anyone: a line learned by heart is a line no exile can carry off.

how: Jews read this promise as part of Jeremiah's chapters of comfort; learning blessings and verses such as the Shema by heart is a familiar part of Jewish education.

games.q: you're promised a new covenant. what does God write, and where?
o: nothing; the law is set aside.
games.why: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts: the same teaching, in a new place.

practice: Choose one line from these days on Jeremiah's road, it was never about your size, or there is hope, or today's: I will write it in their hearts.
Say it slowly, once, under your breath, then close your eyes and say it again without looking. Say it once more on the out-breath, and let it be yours.

wordCard.voice: Torati. Hebrew for "my teaching": Jeremiah's promise of a covenant where it is no longer only on stone or parchment, but inside. Today's word.
